newsitem.title: USA: White House gives Indonesian's letter to Congress.
newsitem.headline: White House gives Indonesian's letter to Congress.

text.p: The White House released to Congress on Tuesday a letter from an Indonesian businessman in which he recommended a direction for President Bill Clinton's Asia policy soon after Clinton took office in 1993.

White House officials said the letter from Mochtar Riady, founder and chairman of Indonesia's Lippo Group, was sent to the House International Relations Committee, chaired by Republican Representative Benjamin Gilman of New York, one of a number of congressional committees looking into questionable Democratic fundraising from foreign sources.

The March 1993 letter, as described by White House officials, urged Clinton to normalise relations with Vietnam. It noted that his company had two managers already in the country exploring business opportunities.

Riady also asked Clinton to maintain China's most-favoured-nation trade status and appealed for Indonesia President Suharto to attend the annual economic summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations.

Clinton ultimately did move to re-establish ties to Vietnam, kept China's trade status and had a private meeting with Suharto. But Clinton said on Monday there was nothing wrong with the letter and that it was one of "tens of thousands" he gets routinely.

"The notion that this letter had any effect on U.S.-Asia policy is not credible," said one White House aide. "Many, many people write the president letters setting forth their views on policy. But frankly this just doesn't have anything to do with the foreign policy process."

But Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said the letter "adds more fuel to the fire" over Democratic fundraising. The Democratic National Committee has returned some $1.5 million in questionable contributions raised by former Lippo associate John Huang, who was an assistant commerce secretary before moving to the DNC as a top fundraiser.

"It raises more questions about ... policy being discussed, and were actions taken based on those recommendations? And is there a connection to the contributions? You've got to look into that," Lott said.
Republicans are vowing to hold hearings on the matter, particularly since Attorney General Janet Reno has refused three requests to name an independent counsel to investigate the matter.

Though Republicans complained of a White House delay in releasing the letter, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the White House has received about 100 requests for related documents from about 11 congressional committees and that many of them are ovelapping.
"We certainly will cooperate and provide the information in a candid and forthright manner," he said.
